problems.title: A quotient of two square roots
problems.question: Find the domain of $\sqrt{x^2-6x+5}/\sqrt{25-x^2}$.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: The numerator radicand must be nonnegative; the denominator radicand must be strictly positive.
steps: (x−1)(x−5)≥0 gives x≤1 or x≥5. The denominator requires −5<x<5.
Their intersection is (−5,1].

problems.title: Transform a function’s range
problems.question: f has range [−5,3]. Find the range of 3f(x)−12.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: A positive multiplier preserves the order of interval endpoints.
steps: Transform the minimum and maximum: 3(−5)−12=−27 and 3×3−12=−3. Both are attained.

problems.title: A coefficient sum is a function value
problems.question: The vertex of y=ax²+bx+c is (1,8), and it passes through (2,−12). Find a+b+c.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
steps: The vertex itself tells us f(1)=8. The other point is not needed for the requested sum.

problems.title: Oddness after adding a square
problems.question: g(x)=f(x)+x² is odd, and f(−5)=1. Find f(5).
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.

problems.title: Pair equal values of an even function
problems.question: f is even and f(3)+f(−5)=7. Evaluate 7f(3)+8f(−5)−2f(−3)−3f(5).
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Evenness gives f(−3)=f(3), f(5)=f(−5).
steps: The expression becomes 5f(3)+5f(−5)=5×7=35.

problems.title: Signs of quadratic coefficients from a graph
problems.question: The source parabola opens downward, has its vertex left of the y axis and crosses the y axis above zero. Find the signs of a,b,c.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: a determines opening; c=f(0); vertex abscissa is −b/(2a).
steps: The opening gives a<0; the positive y intercept gives c>0. Since a<0, the sign of −b/(2a) is the sign of b.
The vertex abscissa is negative, so b<0.

problems.title: A vertex in quadrant two
problems.question: For which a does y=x²−6ax+4+8a² have its vertex in quadrant II?
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Complete the square: y=(x−3a)²+4−a².
steps: The vertex is (3a,4−a²). Require 3a<0 and 4−a²>0, giving −2<a<0.

problems.title: The least coefficient sum for a nonnegative quadratic
problems.question: x²+bx+c is nonnegative for every real x. Minimize b+c.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Nonnegativity requires c≥b²/4.
steps: b+c≥b+b²/4=(b+2)²/4−1≥−1. Equality occurs at b=−2,c=1, giving (x−1)².

problems.title: Integer solutions of two quadratic inequalities
problems.question: Count integer solutions of −2x²−5x+18≥0 and x²+4x−5≤0.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Factor each quadratic and intersect the allowed intervals.
steps: The first holds on [−9/2,2]; the second on [−5,1]. Their intersection is [−9/2,1].
The integers are −4,−3,−2,−1,0,1, six values.

problems.title: A quadratic strictly negative everywhere
problems.question: For which a is ax²+2(1+a)x+9a+4<0 for every real x?
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: A genuine quadratic is strictly negative everywhere iff a<0 and its discriminant is negative.
steps: The discriminant is 4(1−2a−8a²). Requiring it negative gives (4a−1)(2a+1)>0, so a<−1/2 or a>1/4.
Intersect with a<0 to get a<−1/2. At a=0 the expression is linear and cannot be negative everywhere.

problems.title: A vertex at a fixed distance from the origin
problems.question: For y=x²+6x+c, the vertex is distance 5 from the origin. Find c.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: The vertex is (−3,c−9); distance squared = coordinate-square sum.
steps: 9+(c−9)²=25 gives c−9=±4. Thus c=5 or 13.

problems.title: Nearest point on a line
problems.question: Find the point M on 2x−y=5 nearest to A=(−7,1).
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: The perpendicular projection onto ax+by+c=0 is $P-[(aP_x+bP_y+c)/(a^2+b^2)](a,b)$.
steps: The normal is (2,−1), the line expression at A is −20 and its squared norm is 5.
M=(−7,1)−(−4)(2,−1)=(1,−3). It lies on the line and AM is normal to it.

problems.title: Increasing on a prescribed interval
problems.question: For which a is y=x²−2ax+5 increasing on [−3,−2]?
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: The parabola has vertex at x=a and increases to its right.
steps: The entire interval must lie to the right of, or start at, the vertex. Thus a≤−3. Even with a=−3 the function strictly increases between distinct interval inputs.

problems.title: An even part of an arbitrary function
problems.question: f is defined on all reals. What symmetry must f(x)+f(−x) have?
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Evenness means h(−x)=h(x).
steps: Replacing x by −x swaps the two summands and leaves their sum unchanged.

problems.title: Zeros of an odd function
problems.question: An odd function on all reals has exactly two positive zeros. How many zeros altogether?
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Oddness pairs positive and negative zeros and forces f(0)=0.
steps: The two positive zeros have exactly two distinct negative partners. Together with zero, this gives five.

problems.title: Area from incircle pieces of a hypotenuse
problems.question: An incircle divides a right triangle’s hypotenuse into 8 cm and 12 cm. Find its area.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: With inradius r, the legs are 8+r,12+r and hypotenuse 20; area = r times semiperimeter.
steps: (8+r)²+(12+r)²=400 gives r²+20r−96=0, so r=4 (the other root is negative).
The semiperimeter is 20+r=24. Area=4×24=96 cm².

problems.title: Leg sum from two altitude-triangle areas
problems.question: The altitude to a right triangle’s hypotenuse splits it into areas 6 and 54. Find the sum of the legs.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Area ratio equals hypotenuse-piece ratio; leg-square ratio equals those same pieces.
steps: The piece ratio is 1:9, so the leg ratio is 1:3. Write legs t,3t. The whole area is 60, so 3t²/2=60 and t=2√10.
The leg sum is 4t=8√10.

problems.title: Area from two altitudes and the included angle
problems.question: A=30°, and the altitudes from B,C are 2 and 3 cm. Find triangle area.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: h_B=AB sin A and h_C=AC sin A; area=AB·AC sin A/2.

problems.title: The centroid’s triangle along one side
problems.question: Medians meet at K in a triangle of area 24. Find area BKC.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: The centroid’s distance from a side is one third the opposite vertex’s distance.
steps: BKC and BAC have the same base BC and a 1:3 height ratio. Thus area BKC=24/3=8.

problems.title: A parallel cut and an area-ratio wording issue
problems.question: A line parallel to one triangle side divides its area in ratio 16:25. Find the ratio in which it divides an intersected side.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Similar triangles have area ratio equal to the square of their side ratio.
steps: If the smaller triangle has area 16 parts and the remaining trapezoid 25, its fraction of the whole is 16/41. The vertex-to-cut side fraction is 4/√41.
Thus the two side pieces are in ratio 4:(√41−4). If the small triangle instead has 25 parts, the analogous ratio is 5:(√41−5).
The frequently expected 4:5 would compare the small triangle with the whole, which is not what dividing the area into two parts means.
problems.note: None of the printed rational side ratios matches the stated two-part area ratio. The source also does not identify which area is the triangular part.

problems.title: Rectangle sides from a bisected corner triangle
problems.question: A rectangle’s corner-angle bisector divides the opposite diagonal in ratio 1:4. The rectangle area is 36 m². Find its perimeter.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: In the triangle containing that bisector, the angle-bisector theorem gives adjacent-side ratio 1:4.
steps: Write rectangle sides t,4t. The area is 4t²=36, so t=3. Dimensions are 3 by 12 and perimeter 30 m.

problems.title: Distances from an interior point to three sides
problems.question: AB=13,BC=14,AC=15. Interior M is distance 6 from AB and 3 from BC. Find its distance to AC.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Heron’s area and decomposition $S=\tfrac12(13\cdot6+14\cdot3+15d)$.
steps: Semiperimeter is 21 and Heron area √(21×8×7×6)=84. The first two subareas are 39 and 21.
The remaining area is 24=15d/2, so d=48/15=3.2 cm.

problems.title: Two cevians and three known small areas
problems.question: A lies on KL,B on LM and KB meets MA at C. Areas KAC,MBC,KCM are 3,1,3. Find area ALC.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Area ratios along the same line equal base ratios; balanced endpoint masses give inverse division ratios.
steps: Equal KAC,KCM areas give AC=CM. Areas MBC:MKC give BC:CK=1:3.
Assign mass k to K and l to L. Then A has mass k+l. Since AC=CM, M has mass k+l too. B therefore has mass k+2l.
CK:CB=mass(B):mass(K)=3:1 implies k+2l=3k, so l=k. Hence KA=AL.
KAC and ALC share the same altitude to KL and have equal bases KA,AL. Their areas are equal, so ALC=3.

problems.title: A circle diameter creates two altitude feet
problems.question: MN is a circle diameter. K is exterior; segments KM,KN meet the circle at A,B. Area KAB is one quarter of area KMN. Find ANK.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
formulas: Thales gives NA⊥KM and MB⊥KN. If angle MKN=theta, KA=KN cos theta and KB=KM cos theta.
steps: The common-angle area ratio is KA·KB/(KM·KN)=cos²theta=1/4. The segment-foot configuration makes theta acute, so theta=60°.
In right triangle KAN, ANK=90−theta=30°.

problems.title: A perpendicular diagonal line in a rectangle
problems.question: In rectangle ABCD, the perpendicular from B to AC meets AD at M, with MB=MD. BC=9√3. Find its area.
problems.idea: Use the governing formula and check signs, domains and possible configurations.
steps: The perpendicular line has equation y=h−(w/h)x, so M=(h²/w,0). Put m=h²/w.
MB²=m²+h² and MD²=(w−m)². Equality gives h²=w²−2wm=w²−2h², hence h=w/√3.
w=9√3 gives h=9 and area wh=81√3.
